panel: notebook: Under the hood, 'The conversion rules'
what: The notebook promises that Chapter 11 shows sanitizers catching an out-of-range double-to-int conversion. Chapter 11 has no such run, and the course's sanitizer flags can't catch it with g++.
evidence: ch4: "If the whole part doesn't fit the integer type at all, for example 1e20 into an int, the result is undefined behaviour: anything may happen. Chapter 11 shows how sanitizers catch that." cpp/ch11.html has no float-cast-overflow report (grep 'float', 'cannot be represented' finds only the signed-overflow run). Scratch test: `int x = 1e20*argc;` built with capture.py's .san flags (g++ 13.3 -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all) printed -2147483648 and exited 0. GCC leaves -fsanitize=float-cast-overflow out of -fsanitize=undefined.
fix: Replace the last sentence with: "Sanitizers can catch this too, but only when you ask for it by name (g++: -fsanitize=float-cast-overflow)." Or drop the sentence. Don't point to Chapter 11.

what: Two broken promises: Chapter 7 is supposed to move the Light-to-word switch into a function, but cpp/ch7.html has no enum, no Light and no switch at all.
evidence: P18: "To print a word like "red", write a switch that prints it. In Chapter 7 you'll put that switch into a function of its own." P47: "that switch that turns a Light into a word wants to live somewhere of its own. Next time we build functions". grep -c 'Light' cpp/ch7.html = 0 and grep -c 'switch' cpp/ch7.html = 0. Enum-to-string conversion is in cpp/ch20.html.
fix: P18: "Once you can write functions (Chapter 7), a switch like this makes a neat little function of its own; Chapter 20 shows the usual ways to turn an enum into text." P47: replace the Light sentence with a general one, e.g. "Our programs are getting long, and the same steps keep coming back."

what: The question pins the wrong output on the pipe. It says the pipe run printed "Hi Ada, next year you will be 37", but that line came from the `<` redirect. One of the question's own options then says the pipe greeting used Wren and 31.
evidence: q: "With a pipe, the screen showed <samp>Name? Age? Hi Ada, next year you will be 37.</samp> on one line." data/cpp-ch4.json greet.cpp steps: `echo "Wren 30" | ./greet` -> "Name? Age? Hi Wren, next year you will be 31."; `./greet < visitor.txt` -> "...Hi Ada, next year you will be 37." Option why: "It read both: the greeting uses Wren and 31."
fix: Change the q to "With a pipe, the screen showed <samp>Name? Age? Hi Wren, next year you will be 31.</samp> on one line. Why?"

what: The analogy word 'letter' means a whole word or number (one piece of mail). On the same page it also means a single character. Beginners can easily pick up the common misconception that `>>` reads one character.
evidence: P6 Cindy: "Before each >> I sweep aside spaces... Then I take one letter." P7: "one tile per letter (a word or number)". Recap: "ONE LETTER AT A TIME ... A string gets one word." ex-filltwo explain: "takes the first letter for bolts and the next one for nuts". The same page uses 'letter' as a character: P16 title "letters where a number should be", Cindy "A number can't start with a!", P35 "Each letter has a code: A is 65".
fix: Use 'envelope' or 'item' for the mail sense, e.g. P6 "Then I take one item", recap "ONE ITEM AT A TIME", ex-filltwo "takes the first item for bolts". Keep 'letter' for characters only. (The newline is already 'the envelope', so 'item' or 'parcel' fits better.)

what: The double card says the read stops at anything other than digits and one decimal point. The chapter's own notebook says an optional sign and an exponent are read too.
evidence: P8: "Digits with one decimal point, like 3.7 or .5. Stops at anything else." Notebook: "digits, one point and an exponent like e5 for a double".
fix: "An optional sign, digits and one decimal point (like 3.7 or .5), even an exponent like 1e3. Stops at anything else."

what: The type `long` is used in three places without ever being introduced. Chapter 3 doesn't introduce it either.
evidence: cstyle.cpp `long sneaky = (long)"42";`, named_cast.cpp `static_cast<long>("42")`, machine example `static_cast<long>("42")`. grep 'long' in cpp/ch3.html finds no type use.
fix: Add one clause in P37: "(`long` is a bigger cousin of `int`, big enough to hold a memory address here)", and add `long` to Words from this chapter.

what: Compiler messages are quoted that no captured program produced: g++'s narrowing message for `int a{3.0};`, the refusal of `bool on{2};`, and `(int)"42"` being an error.
evidence: ex-lid-m why: "g++ says narrowing conversion of ‘3.0e+0’ from ‘double’ to ‘int’". Notebook: "`(int)"42"` ... It's an error". data/cpp-ch4.json has none of these programs. I checked them in scratch with g++ 13.3, and all three claims hold ("narrowing conversion of '3.0e+0'", "narrowing conversion of '2' from 'int' to 'bool'", "cast from 'const char*' to 'int' loses precision [-fpermissive]"). So they're true, but nothing on the page backs them up.
fix: Capture lid_three.cpp (`int a{3.0};`), lid_bool.cpp (`bool on{2};`) and cast_int.cpp (`(int)"42"`), and show or link the real messages. Otherwise drop the quoted wording ("g++ refuses it").

panel: 12 (Wren bubble), notebook 'Short strings live inside the box'
what: The page says a sanitizer run of `"hello"[10]` was tried and reported nothing. That run isn't captured or shown, and the footer says every terminal comes from a real run without saying this one is described only.
evidence: P12: "we tried \"hello\" and seat 10 with the same goggles, and they reported nothing." No such program in data/cpp-ch5.json (walk_off.cpp is the only .san). Scratch check with the same flags confirms it: there is no report, and the program prints the UB byte (0) with exit 0. So it's true, but capturing it would mean showing UB as output.
fix: Add to the footer: "Panel 12's 'hello' seat-10 sanitizer run is described, not shown: the sanitizer stays silent there, so the run would only print an undefined value."

what: The parsons prompt asks the reader to put the #include lines in alphabetical order. That's a convention, not logic, and the engine can now pin those lines.
evidence: prompt: "(Headers go first, in alphabetical order, then a blank line.)" boss_password.cpp lines 1-2 are `#include <iostream>` and `#include <string>`. The model has no "pin". AUTHORING engine note: 'Parsons: blank lines and pinned lines'.
fix: Add "pin": [1, 2] to ex-b3-m and drop the parenthesis from the prompt.
